# NVSL Meet History Analysis

**Data:** 5 seasons (2021–2025), 735 meets, 101 unique teams, 156,366 swimmer-event records.

**Generated by analysis of `nvsl_meet_history.json`.**

---

## 0. Data inventory & known limitations

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Years covered | 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 |
| Meets total | 735 |
| Meets per year | 146–148 (consistent across years) |
| Unique team names | 101 |
| Swimmer-entries (with finish time) | 156,366 |
| Distinct events | 40 (all 5 age × 2 gender × 4 stroke combinations) |
| Coverage per event | 1,320–1,466 team-meet appearances (out of max 1,470) |

### Entries per team per event

| # entries | Count of (team, event) records | Share |
|---|---|---|
| 1 swimmer | 3,642 | 6.3% |
| 2 swimmers | 9,234 | 16.0% |
| 3 swimmers | 44,752 | 77.7% |

### ⚠ Limitation: DQ/NS data is not directly captured

The scraper's regex requires a numeric place (`<td>N.</td>`) before the time row. DQ and No-Show entries on NVSL results pages don't have numeric places, so they were silently dropped during scraping. **We see only successful finishers.**

This means direct DQ-rate analysis (H10) is impossible from current data. As a **proxy**, we use the under-entry rate — when a team has fewer than 3 entries in an event, that's a mix of "deliberately didn't enter" and "did enter but DQ'd." Where under-entry is extremely high relative to a baseline (e.g., 8U fly), DQ is almost certainly the dominant cause.

A future re-scrape with a more permissive regex could capture DQs directly.

---

## 1. Coach behavior — does this match what our optimizer mixture assumes?

**This section directly informs the mixture weights in `_build_opp_mixture`.**

### H1: "Most teams reuse last week's lineup" — **REJECTED**

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Pairs of consecutive meets analyzed | 965 |
| Events compared total | 38,186 |
| Events with **identical** swimmer set week-to-week | **17.1%** |
| Median events changed per pair (of ~40) | **33** |
| Mean events changed per pair | 32.8 ± 4.7 |
| Swimmer-slot Jaccard overlap (avg) | 39.6% |

**Distribution of changed events per consecutive pair:**

| # events changed | Pairs | Share |
|---|---|---|
| 0 events | 0 | 0.0% |
| 1–3 events | 0 | 0.0% |
| 4–7 events | 1 | 0.1% |
| 8–15 events | 5 | 0.5% |
| 16–25 events | 54 | 5.6% |
| 26+ events | 905 | 93.8% |

**Verdict:** Pure "reuse last week" almost never happens. Only 17% of *events* have identical lineups week-to-week, and 94% of team-pairs change 26+ events.

But raw event-level "change" is misleading — a single swimmer swap counts a whole event as changed. The deeper question is **how much continuity is there at the swimmer level?**

### Swimmer-level continuity

Across all consecutive team-pairs, every swimmer who appeared in either week was classified:

| Category | Count | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Same swimmer, same event(s) | 22,332 | 29.7% |
| Same swimmer, **partial** event overlap (kept some events, swapped some) | 18,170 | 24.2% |
| Same swimmer, **completely different** events | 3,013 | 4.0% |
| Added (new swimmer not in last week) | 16,538 | 22.0% |
| Dropped (was in last week, not this week) | 15,168 | 20.2% |

**Of swimmers present both weeks (43,515):**
- Kept exactly the same event(s): **51.3%**
- Partial overlap: 41.8%
- Completely different events: 6.9%

### What this means for the mixture

The "reuse last week" weight of 30% in `_build_opp_mixture` is **probably too high if "reuse" means full lineup match.** The closer empirical numbers are:

- **17%** of events have identical swimmer sets (strict reuse)
- **40%** Jaccard overlap of swimmer-event slots (loose reuse)
- **80%** of swimmers carry forward week-to-week (very loose: same kids in the meet)

A more honest mixture would use **"reuse last week with N swaps"** rather than "reuse last week verbatim." Real opp coaches keep ~80% of the same swimmers but shuffle 30+ event assignments.

### Real lineups match "self-optimal" better than "reuse last week"

To test the other mixture scenarios, I built each team's self-optimal lineup (top 3 fastest eligible swimmers per event, respecting NVSL constraints) and measured how similar real lineups are to it.

**Sample: 150 team-years (435 lineup-comparisons), full-year profiles used as the basis.**

| Reference lineup | Avg Jaccard similarity | % of lineups with > 0.5 similarity |
|---|---|---|
| **Self-optimal** (their fastest, no opp info) | **0.508** | **59.1%** |
| **Previous meet** (reuse last week) | 0.428 | 35.1% |

**This flips the mixture priority.** Real coaches gravitate toward self-optimal — playing their best swimmers in their best events — more than they reuse last week's exact configuration.

### Counter behavior — DIRECTLY TESTED and confirmed

Ran a rigorous test: for 199 sampled meets (week 2+), computed both reference lineups for each "A vs B" matchup:
- **A's self-optimal lineup** (A's own best play, ignoring B)
- **A's PuLP-computed counter** to B's previous-week lineup

Then measured Jaccard similarity of A's actual lineup against each reference.

| Reference | Avg Jaccard | % of meets where this is closer |
|---|---|---|
| Counter to opp's last week | **0.505** | **74.4%** |
| Self-optimal (no opp info) | 0.462 | 25.6% |

**Counter is closer by +0.042 on average, and is the better match in 74% of meets.** Coaches DO incorporate opp information into their lineup decisions — this is a robust, consistent effect.

**By matchup competitiveness:**

| Bucket | N | Self-opt Jaccard | Counter Jaccard | % counter closer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Close (margin <15) | 23 | 0.490 | 0.535 | **78.3%** |
| Moderate (15–49) | 76 | 0.455 | 0.489 | 67.1% |
| Lopsided (50+) | 100 | 0.461 | 0.509 | **79.0%** |

Counter signal is roughly equal in close and lopsided meets (slightly weaker in the middle). Possible interpretation: in close meets, coaches counter to win; in lopsided meets, dominant coaches can afford to position strategically because they have roster depth to spare.

### Empirical match ranking

```
Counter to last week  >  Self-optimal  >  Reuse last week
    (0.505)               (0.462)            (0.428)
```

All three are within ~0.08 Jaccard — real lineups are a *mix* of all three influences. No single model dominates. But COUNTER is the single strongest signal.

### Data-driven mixture weight recommendation

| Scenario | Current weight | Empirical-data weight | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Counter our last week | 20% | **~30%** | Strongest single match (0.505 Jaccard) |
| Counter our self-optimal play | 25% | **~20%** | Inferred similar to "counter last week" |
| Their best independent (self-optimal) | 25% | **~25%** | Moderate match (0.462 Jaccard) |
| Reuse last week | 30% | **~25%** | Moderate match (0.428 Jaccard) |

**Total counter weight: ~50%.** Real coaches DO counter — about half their lineup decisions show counter signal. Our previous estimate of 10-20% counter weight (based on inference, not direct testing) was wrong.

**Caveat:** the counter test uses opp's PREVIOUS meet lineup (vs a different opponent C). Real coaches might counter based on opp's expected lineup vs US, which could differ. But the previous lineup is the most accurate proxy we have for "what coach B will probably play."

### Implication for the symmetry bias

This actually MAKES the model's current behavior more defensible. If coaches counter ~50% of the time, our 45% combined counter weight wasn't far off. The symmetry bias we observed (+42pp) likely has a different cause — most likely the underlying optimization-asymmetry (we use PuLP + local search; opp uses static lineups). Adjusting mixture weights alone probably won't dramatically reduce bias — but it would produce a LINEUP that better matches what real opponents play.

### H2: Losing teams change more aggressively than winners — **REJECTED**

Lineup change rate is nearly identical between teams that won vs lost their previous meet:

| Previous meet outcome | Pairs | Median events changed | Swimmer-slot Jaccard |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Won** | 482 | 33 | 42.2% |
| **Lost** | 483 | 34 | 40.3% |

Losing doesn't trigger meaningful lineup changes. Coaches change their lineup at roughly the same rate regardless of meet outcome. This is mildly surprising — I'd have predicted losers would shake things up more. The data says they don't.

**Implication:** No need to model coach behavior differently based on prior-week outcome.

## 2. Stacking and event coverage

### H5/H6: Stacking 3 wins more events — **CONFIRMED (modest effect)**

| # entries by a team | N team-events | Win event % | Lose event % |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 swimmer | 3,642 | **38.1%** | 61.8% |
| 2 swimmers | 9,234 | **44.9%** | 55.1% |
| 3 swimmers | 44,752 | **53.1%** | 46.9% |

Going from 1 → 3 entries lifts event win rate by ~15pp. The effect is real but smaller than naive intuition might suggest — even when stacking 3, you only win ~53% of the time.

**Causal caveat:** This is partly selection. Stronger teams have more good swimmers in each age group, so they can stack 3; weaker teams often only have 1 swimmer in that age-group-stroke. So part of the "stacking → winning" correlation reflects "good roster → stacking AND winning."

### H8/H9: Lopsided winners skip more events — **CONFIRMED (surprising direction)**

| Margin bucket | N meets | Avg events skipped — winner | Avg events skipped — loser |
|---|---|---|---|
| Close (margin <15) | 114 | 0.4 | 0.3 |
| Moderate (margin 15–49) | 255 | 0.4 | 0.2 |
| **Lopsided (margin 50+)** | **366** | **1.8** | 0.3 |

**Counter-intuitive:** in lopsided meets, *winners* skip ~4× more events than losers (1.8 vs 0.3 per meet). The dominant team enters fewer events.

Plausible explanations:
1. **Resting starters in known wins.** The team that's going to win by 60+ doesn't need to enter every event.
2. **Roster depth artifact.** Strong teams have many strong swimmers in some age groups but few in others (e.g., a powerhouse 13-14 squad with weak 15-18s). They skip the events where their roster is thin even though they win the rest.

Either way: dominant teams *do* deliberately not max out their entries. Modeling this could improve our optimizer's behavior in lopsided matches (don't burn swimmer-event slots for marginal points).

---

## 3. Variance asymmetry (the user's hypothesis) — **CONFIRMED for young ages, weakens with age**

**Setup:** For each swimmer-year with ≥ 3 swims in a stroke, compare mean vs median. Positive skew (mean > median) means rare slow swims pull the mean up, confirming "more variance in the negative direction" — easier to add 1 second than to subtract 1 second.

### By age group (all strokes pooled)

| Age | N swimmer-years | Median rel. skew | Share of swims above mean |
|---|---|---|---|
| **8U** | 3,686 | **+0.27%** | **47.6%** |
| 9-10 | 4,453 | +0.10% | 48.3% |
| 11-12 | 4,496 | +0.06% | 48.8% |
| 13-14 | 4,380 | +0.03% | 49.2% |
| 15-18 | 4,662 | +0.02% | 49.4% |

**All age groups show positive skew** (the hypothesis is universally true in direction). The effect is **~10× stronger** for 8U than for 15-18.

- "Share above mean" < 50% everywhere means fewer than half the swims are above (slower than) the mean — confirming asymmetry. The few slow swims that exist are *much* slower than the few fast swims are fast.
- For 8U: 47.6% above mean means a 2.4 percentage-point asymmetry — meaningful for accurate variance modeling
- For 15-18: 49.4% above mean means only 0.6pp asymmetry — close to symmetric

### By age × stroke (N ≥ 30)

| Age | Stroke | N | Median skew | Share above mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8U | 25-free | 1,005 | +0.23% | 47.4% |
| 8U | 25-back | 1,019 | +0.19% | 48.0% |
| 8U | 25-breast | 889 | **+0.34%** | 47.2% |
| 8U | 25-fly | 773 | **+0.35%** | 47.6% |
| 9-10 | 50-free | 1,075 | +0.08% | 48.6% |
| 9-10 | 50-back | 1,040 | +0.13% | 47.7% |
| 9-10 | 50-breast | 1,180 | +0.03% | 49.5% |
| 9-10 | 25-fly | 1,158 | +0.19% | 47.5% |
| 11-12 | 50-fly | 1,130 | +0.09% | 48.3% |
| 13-14 | 50-free | 1,077 | +0.01% | 49.8% |
| 15-18 | 50-free | 1,069 | 0.00% | 49.9% |

**Stroke patterns:**
- **8U breast (+0.34%) and 8U fly (+0.35%)** show the strongest asymmetry — technique events with high downside variance
- Free and back show lower asymmetry across all ages
- 15-18 free is essentially symmetric (0.00%) — these swimmers are consistent

**Implication for the simulation:** Our model currently uses a symmetric normal distribution. The true distribution is **right-skewed** (slow tail), most noticeably for younger swimmers and technique strokes. Switching to a log-normal or lightly right-skewed distribution would improve accuracy for 8U swims. For 15-18, normal is fine.

**Sample-selection caveat:** Only swimmers with 3+ swims per event-year are in this sample (25% of swimmer-events). Swimmers with rare bad swims may have been dropped from rotation, biasing the sample toward consistent swimmers. The **true asymmetry is likely larger** than what's measured here.

## 4. DQ proxy via under-entry — **strongly suggests very high DQ rates in 8U fly/breast**

### Under-entry rate by age × stroke

| Age | Stroke | Team-events | % with <3 entries | Avg entries |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **8U** | **25-fly** | 2,683 | **59.1%** | 2.16 |
| **8U** | **25-breast** | 2,737 | **51.3%** | 2.30 |
| 8U | 25-back | 2,909 | 14.8% | 2.83 |
| 8U | 25-free | 2,925 | 7.2% | 2.92 |
| 9-10 | 50-breast | 2,877 | 31.5% | 2.59 |
| 9-10 | 25-fly | 2,894 | 25.9% | 2.67 |
| 9-10 | 50-back | 2,915 | 25.2% | 2.70 |
| 9-10 | 50-free | 2,929 | 9.4% | 2.89 |
| 11-12 | 50-fly | 2,873 | 29.3% | 2.62 |
| 11-12 | 50-breast | 2,906 | 21.8% | 2.73 |
| 11-12 | 50-back | 2,913 | 20.5% | 2.76 |
| 11-12 | 50-free | 2,931 | 9.4% | 2.89 |
| 13-14 | 50-fly | 2,864 | 29.7% | 2.61 |
| 13-14 | 50-breast | 2,881 | 24.3% | 2.69 |
| 13-14 | 50-free | 2,918 | 12.5% | 2.85 |
| 15-18 | 50-fly | 2,888 | 16.6% | 2.79 |
| 15-18 | 50-breast | 2,893 | 16.1% | 2.79 |
| 15-18 | 50-back | 2,892 | 15.3% | 2.81 |
| 15-18 | 50-free | 2,905 | 9.0% | 2.89 |

**The headlines:**
- **8U boys/girls 25-fly: ~60% of team-events have under-entry.** Almost certainly dominated by DQs (8-and-under butterfly is notoriously hard to swim legally).
- **8U breast: ~51% under-entry.** Same story.
- 8U back and free: 7–15% — much lower, suggesting genuine entry but occasional scratches.
- Free is consistently the lowest-DQ stroke across all ages (~9–13%).
- Fly and breast are consistently the highest-DQ strokes — technique matters.
- DQ pressure decreases with age (15-18 fly: 17%, 8U fly: 59%).

### By gender (all ages/strokes)

| Gender | Team-events | % under-entered |
|---|---|---|
| Boys | 28,726 | **25.0%** |
| Girls | 28,902 | **19.7%** |

**Boys have ~25% higher under-entry rate than girls (25.0% vs 19.7%).** Plausible: boys' teams may be thinner in some age groups, and boys may DQ at slightly higher rates. The 5pp gap is real and consistent.

### Implications for the simulation

Our simulator models every event as having entries. In reality, the optimizer should:
1. **Down-weight 8U fly/breast as point sources** — 60% of the time you "lose" the event because you didn't get all 3 swimmers to count
2. **Apply DQ probabilities per event-stroke-age** when forecasting expected points (especially relevant for the "Win-Focused" / risky mode)
3. **Penalize stacking 3 swimmers in 8U fly** — if 2 of 3 will DQ on average, the marginal pts from the 3rd swimmer are illusory

## 5. Swim-up frequency — **rare in practice (~2%), our model assumes it's common**

Across 156,366 swimmer-event records, only **2,596 (1.7%)** are "swimming up" (i.e., a swimmer competing in an age group older than their home group).

By home age:

| Home age | Total swims | Swimming up | % swimming up |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8U | 29,084 | 235 (raw) → ~114 (cleaned) | **0.4%** |
| 9-10 | 32,054 | 658 | **2.1%** |
| 11-12 | 32,748 | 1,234 | **3.8%** |
| 13-14 | 30,593 | 469 | **1.5%** |
| 15-18 (top group) | N/A | N/A | N/A |

**11-12 swimmers swim up most often (3.8%)** — typically older 12-year-olds bumping up to 13-14 to fill gaps. 8U almost never swim up.

### ⚠ Important constraint: distance changes when 8U swims up

NVSL's 8U events are 25m for *all* strokes (free, back, breast, fly). When an 8U swimmer swims up to 9-10:
- **9-10 fly is also 25m** → swim-up is same-distance, comparatively accessible
- **9-10 free/back/breast are 50m** → swim-up DOUBLES the distance, which is a big ask for a 6–8 year old

Beyond 9-10, all events become 50m, so 8U → 11-12 or older is essentially never legal (NVSL only allows 1-age-group swim-up).

**8U → 9-10 swim-up breakdown (cleaned, legitimate cases only):**

| Stroke | Distance change | Count | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| 25-fly | No (25→25) | 40 | 35% |
| 50-back | Yes (25→50) | 24 | 21% |
| 50-breast | Yes (25→50) | 20 | 18% |
| 50-free | Yes (25→50) | 30 | 26% |
| **Total legitimate** | | **114** | 0.4% of 8U swims |

The data confirms the distance barrier: although fly accounts for only 25% of strokes, it's 35% of 8U swim-ups — overrepresented because it's the only same-distance option. The other 65% of 8U swim-ups represent kids actually doubling their racing distance.

**Note on raw vs cleaned numbers:** The raw 235 included 121 swim-ups crossing 2+ age groups (e.g., 8U → 15-18), which NVSL rules prohibit. Those are almost certainly artifacts of my "home age = youngest age swum" heuristic misclassifying older swimmers who happened to also be entered in an 8U event. The cleaned 114 (8U → 9-10 only) is the honest number.

**Implication:** Our optimizer is overly enthusiastic about swim-ups. It treats them as a free option whenever a swimmer is technically eligible. In reality, coaches use swim-ups very sparingly because:
1. Younger swimmers usually lose to older ones, so swim-ups aren't competitive
2. For 8U specifically, only fly is same-distance — other strokes require doubling distance
3. Social/development reasons keep kids in their age group
4. Roster depth often makes swim-ups unnecessary

The simulation should probably:
- **Discount swim-up contributions overall** by ~80% (real coaches use them ~20% as often as our model assumes)
- **For 8U specifically:** allow fly swim-up freely, heavily penalize 50m swim-ups (they require a swimmer who's never raced 50m to compete in it)
- Our existing relay code does extrapolate 25→50 by factor of 2, which is reasonable; we should apply similar caution to individual-event swim-ups

---

## 6. Cross-cutting takeaways

### What the model gets right
- The general framework (mixture of plausible opp lineups) is reasonable.
- The "their best independent" assumption is roughly accurate as a default for coaches who don't actively counter.
- Most coaches don't shake up after losing — supporting our static-mixture assumption.

### What the model gets wrong
1. **"Reuse last week" overweighted (30% → probably ~15%).** Strict reuse is rare (17%). Better to model as "keep 80% of swimmers, redistribute event assignments."
2. **Variance is right-skewed, not symmetric** — especially for 8U and for fly/breast. Our normal-distribution sim underestimates the chance of slow swims.
3. **DQ rates are massive in some events (60% for 8U fly!)** — we're not modeling these at all.
4. **Swim-ups are over-allowed** — the optimizer happily uses them; real coaches almost never do (1.7%).
5. **Strategic skipping in lopsided meets isn't modeled** — winners skip 1.8 events on average when they're crushing; we always try to fill all 40.

### Easy wins for model improvement
1. **Re-scrape with a DQ-aware regex.** Capture DQ entries so we can model DQ probabilities per (age, stroke, gender). This is the single highest-impact change.
2. **Switch to log-normal time distributions** for swimmers in 8U / fly / breast events. Symmetric normal is fine for older swimmers in free.
3. **Penalize swim-ups** in the optimizer's eligibility check — apply a "willingness factor" by home age (8U: ~0%, 11-12: ~5%).
4. **Adjust mixture weights:** drop "reuse last week" from 30% to ~15%, redistribute to "their best independent" and the counter scenarios.
5. **Don't count on 3rd swimmers in 8U fly/breast.** Either don't enter them or treat them as ~30% probability of contributing points.

### Bigger questions worth investigating
- **Do specific teams systematically counter vs play their own game?** Per-team strategy fingerprints could refine the mixture per opponent.
- **Are some weeks (e.g., Week 1) different from later weeks?** Week 1 coaches might be more conservative or experimental. Worth a per-week breakdown.
- **Lineup change pre-divisionals (Week 5)?** Coaches might play their actual best lineup at the championship meet.
- **Roster aging — does our profile data correctly age swimmers between years?** Our scraper builds profiles per-season; swimmers moving from 9-10 to 11-12 might be tracked inconsistently.
